resources.string: How pancreatic ducts help buffer stomach acid
A qualitative view of normal human digestion, from a signal in the duodenum to bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreatic ducts. Structures, timing and moving marks are schematic.
Follow an acinus into a duct

An acinus is a cluster of cells that releases digestive enzymes and their precursors into a shared space. That space drains into a small duct. Cells lining the duct have a different job: they add bicarbonate-rich fluid.
When acidic contents from the stomach reach the duodenum, S cells in its lining release the hormone secretin into the blood. The blood carries the signal to the pancreatic duct cells.
Secretin stimulates duct cells to move bicarbonate into the duct lumen, the space inside the duct. Water follows. The duct cells add this fluid, not the digestive enzymes supplied by acinar cells.
Pancreatic juice flows to the duodenum
Small ducts drain into larger ducts. The main pancreatic duct carries the combined pancreatic juice to the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.
Pancreatic juice mixes with acidic stomach contents in the duodenum. Bicarbonate helps neutralize some of the acid, making the contents less acidic.
